Boeing’s 2023 Form 10-K reports these percentages of its **total workforce** as of **December 31, 2023**:

| Percentage | Union or employee group |
|---|---|

Apple’s fiscal 2024 Form 10-K specifically identifies **three regional net-sales results and two Products gross-margin measures** as unfavorably affected:

| Reported result | Fiscal 2024 vs. fiscal 2023 | Currency weakness cited |
|---|---|---|
| **Greater China net sales** | $66.952 billion vs. $72.559 billion; down 8% | Weakness of the **renminbi** against the U.S. dollar. |
| **Japan net sales** | $25.052 billion vs. $24.257 billion; up 3% | Weakness of the **yen** against the U.S. dollar. |
| **Rest of Asia Pacific net sales** | $30.658 billion vs. $29.615 billion; up 4% | Weakness of **foreign currencies** against the U.S. dollar had a **net unfavorable** year-over-year impact. |
| **Products gross margin** | $109.633 billion vs. $108.803 billion | Foreign-currency weakness against the U.S. dollar partially offset the benefit of cost savings. |
| **Products gross margin percentage** | 37.2% vs. 36.5% | Foreign-currency weakness against the U.S. dollar partially offset the benefit of cost savings. |

Thus, an unfavorable currency effect did **not** necessarily mean the reported result declined; several increased despite that headwind.

**Sources:** Apple fiscal 2024 Form 10-K, Item 7, “Segment Operating Performance,” printed p. 22 (PDF p. 25), and “Products Gross Margin,” printed p. 24 (PDF p. 27).

Apple’s fiscal 2025 Form 10-K reports **six relevant percentages**:

### Share of fiscal 2025 total net sales

| Percentage | What it measures |
|---|---|
| **40%** | Net sales through Apple’s **direct distribution channels**. |
| **60%** | Net sales through **indirect distribution channels**, such as third-party cellular network carriers and other resellers. |

*Source: “Markets and Distribution,” report p. 2 (PDF p. 5).*

### Share of receivables as of September 27, 2025

| Percentage | What it measures |
|---|---|
| **12%** | The share of **total trade receivables** attributable to **one customer**, which Apple does not name. |
| **34%** | The share of **total trade receivables** attributable collectively to **third-party cellular network carriers**. |
| **46%** | The share of **total vendor non-trade receivables** attributable to **one of two individually significant vendors**. |
| **23%** | The share of **total vendor non-trade receivables** attributable to **the other vendor**. |

*Source: “Accounts Receivable,” report p. 39 (PDF p. 42).*

The vendor non-trade receivables arise from **component sales to manufacturing vendors**. Those component sales are not included in Apple’s products net sales, so the **46% and 23% measure receivables concentrations—not sales shares**.

Excluding exhibits, Boeing’s 2024 Form 10-K gives **four distinct dividend dollar amounts** for this preferred stock:

| Amount | What it represents |
|---|---|
| **Up to $345 million per year** | The cash Boeing expects to require annually for preferred dividends through the mandatory conversion date, **October 15, 2027**. Dividends may instead be paid in common shares, subject to limitations, or a combination of cash and shares. *(Risk Factors, printed p. 17; PDF p. 19.)* |
| **$58 million** | Preferred dividends **accumulated during 2024**, deducted in determining the loss attributable to common shareholders and in calculating earnings per share. *(Consolidated Statements of Operations, printed p. 54; Note 4, printed p. 73; PDF pp. 56 and 77.)* |
| **$72 million** | The aggregate dividends **declared in December 2024** for holders of record on January 1, 2025, and **paid in cash on January 15, 2025**. The equity statement also records this declaration. *(Consolidated Statements of Equity, printed p. 58; Note 19, printed p. 106; PDF pp. 62 and 110.)* |
| **$12.50 per preferred share** | The per-share amount of that same December-declared dividend paid January 15, 2025—not a separate dividend payment. *(Note 19, printed p. 106; PDF p. 110.)* |

Thus, **$58 million is the 2024 accumulated-dividend amount**, while **$72 million and $12.50 per share describe the same declared dividend on aggregate and per-share bases**.

The filing specifies **four dates or months in calendar 2025**, covering these developments:

| Date stated | Matter | What happened |
|---|---|---|
| **April 23, 2025** | **EU Digital Markets Act—Article 5(4) investigation** | The European Commission fined Apple **€500 million** and issued a cease-and-desist order requiring it to remove technical and commercial restrictions preventing developers from steering users to alternative distribution channels outside the App Store. [1] |
| **April 23, 2025** | **EU Digital Markets Act—Article 6(4) investigation** | The Commission issued **preliminary findings** in its investigation into whether Apple’s new contractual requirements for third-party app developers and app marketplaces violate the DMA. [1] |
| **April 30, 2025** | **Epic Games litigation** | The Northern District of California found Apple **in violation of the 2021 injunction**. It barred commissions or fees on purchases outside an app, restrictions on developers directing consumers to outside purchases, and interference with consumers’ purchasing choices. It also denied Apple’s motion to narrow or vacate the injunction and referred Apple to the U.S. Attorney for a determination of whether criminal-contempt proceedings were appropriate. [1] |
| **September 2, 2025** | **Google antitrust litigation—relevant to Apple’s search-licensing relationships** | The District of Columbia federal district court **ordered remedies** following the finding that Google violated U.S. antitrust laws. The filing notes that the order remained subject to further proceedings and appeal. [2] |
| **October 2025** *(month only)* | **Epic Games appeal** | The Ninth Circuit **heard oral arguments** in Apple’s expedited appeal of the district court’s ruling. [1] |

**Sources:**  
[1] *AAPL_2025_10K.pdf*, Item 3, “Legal Proceedings,” printed p. 18 (PDF p. 21).  
[2] *AAPL_2025_10K.pdf*, Item 1A, “Risk Factors,” printed p. 14 (PDF p. 17).

The filing also mentions settlements during fiscal 2025’s fourth quarter, but supplies no specific day or month for those settlements.

Boeing’s 2025 Form 10-K gives the following figures, with distinct meanings:

| Figure or date | What it refers to |
|---|---|
| **Approximately 3,200 employees** | The Boeing employees represented by **IAM District 837 at its St. Louis-area sites**—an approximate represented headcount, not an exact tally of strikers or voters. |
| **101 days** | The duration of the **2025 strike**, which disrupted Boeing’s St. Louis operations. |
| **August 4, 2025** | The date the work stoppage began. |
| **November 13, 2025** | The date IAM District 837 members **voted to ratify a new contract**, thereby ending the work stoppage. |
| **July 2030** | The **expiration month and year of the current IAM District 837 collective bargaining agreement**. The agreement table lists its principal location as **Missouri**; it does not provide an exact expiration day. |

Thus, **101 days is the strike’s duration, not the contract’s term**, and **July 2030 is the agreement’s expiration, not the strike’s end date**. The table’s **25% of total workforce** figure applies to **IAM overall**, not District 837 alone.

**Sources:** *BA_2025_10K.pdf*, “Human Capital,” printed p. 2 (PDF p. 4); and MD&A, “Overview,” printed p. 24 (PDF p. 26).

NVIDIA’s **fiscal 2024 Form 10-K** reports these four relevant amounts:

| Fiscal 2024 amount | What it represents | Filing reference |
|---|---|---|
| **$2.2 billion** | Total provisions for inventory and excess inventory purchase obligations, before the related provision releases. | “Gross Profit and Gross Margin,” p. 40 |
| **$774 million** | Inventory provision recorded in cost of revenue—the inventory write-down component, covering excess or obsolete inventory under NVIDIA’s inventory policy. | Note 10, p. 68; inventory policy, p. 58 |
| **Approximately $1.4 billion** | Expense recorded in cost of revenue for **inventory purchase obligations exceeding current demand projections, supplier charges, and penalties related to cancellations and underutilization**. | Note 10, p. 70, footnote (1) |

The filing gives a combined amount, without separately quantifying those two sources. | “Gross Profit and Gross Margin,” p. 40 |

The **$774 million** and **approximately $1.4 billion** are components of the rounded **$2.2 billion total**, not additional charges. The **$540 million** is a release, rather than another charge.

Pfizer’s 2021 Form 10-K gives these separation-cost figures:

| Figure as stated | What it represents |
|---|---|
| **“approximately $700 million”** | Expected **total costs** of separating Upjohn, including costs and expenses related to separating legal entities and transaction costs. |
| **“approximately 75%”** | The portion of those expected costs already incurred **“since inception and through December 31, 2021.”** |
| **“$434 million”** | Separation-related costs incurred **in 2020**. |
| **“$83 million”** | Separation-related costs incurred **in 2019**. |

The first two figures appear in **MD&A—Our Business and Strategy, printed p. 26 (PDF p. 32)**.

The annual amounts appear in **Note 2B—Upjohn Separation and Combination with Mylan, printed p. 65 (PDF p. 71)**. Pfizer says these costs primarily related to professional fees for regulatory filings and separation activities within finance, tax, legal and information-system functions, as well as investment-banking fees. They were included in **“Discontinued operations––net of tax.”**

NVIDIA’s fiscal 2023 Form 10-K describes the following effects:

**Effects that occurred**
1. **Blocked products, services, and support.** U.S. and other jurisdictions’ economic sanctions and export-control measures imposed in response to the war blocked the passage of NVIDIA’s products, services, and support into **Russia, Belarus, and certain regions of Ukraine**. *(Item 1A, p. 28.)*
2. **Stopped direct sales to Russia.** NVIDIA stopped those sales during fiscal 2023. *(Item 1A, p. 28; MD&A, “Russia,” p. 37.)*
3. **Closed its Russian business operations.** NVIDIA closed those operations later in fiscal 2023. *(MD&A, “Russia,” p. 37.)*
4. **Affected end-customer sales in EMEA—Europe, the Middle East, and Africa.** The filing says the war “has impacted” those sales, without quantifying the impact or expressly characterizing its direction in that statement. *(Item 1A, p. 28.)*

**Effect that possibly occurred**
5. **Negatively affected revenue from partners selling into Russia.** NVIDIA says its “revenue to partners that sell into Russia may have been negatively impacted due to the war in Ukraine.” This is a qualified statement about a possible past impact, not merely a future risk. *(MD&A, “Russia,” p. 37.)*

For context, NVIDIA also states that its **direct sales to Russia in fiscal 2022 were immaterial**. *(p. 37.)*

| Amount | What it represents | Filing reference |

These are **overlapping total and component disclosures**, not six amounts to add together. The table excludes the cumulative year-end gain/loss balances, fiscal 2024 figures, and the total of *Other, net*, as requested.

*Source: NVIDIA, fiscal 2025 Form 10-K (`NVDA_2025_10K.pdf`).*

JPMorgan Chase’s **2023 Form 10-K reports a Firmwide allowance reduction of $587 million and an after-tax retained-earnings increase of $446 million** from adopting the TDR guidance. It also gives portfolio and business-segment amounts.

**All amounts below are in millions of dollars.** Minus signs indicate decreases; page references are the report’s printed page numbers.

| Scope and account | Change | What the amount measures | Source |
|---|---:|---|---|
| **Firmwide allowance for credit losses** | **−587** | Net cumulative adoption adjustment, predominantly driven by residential real estate and credit cards. The allowance roll-forward reports the same amount as the total adjustment to the **allowance for loan losses**. | Note 1, p. 173; Note 13, pp. 256, 258 |
| **Consumer, excluding credit card—allowance for loan losses** | **−489** | Cumulative adoption adjustment for this loan portfolio—not a separately identified residential-real-estate-only amount. | Note 13, p. 258 |
| **Credit card—allowance for loan losses** | **−100** | Cumulative adoption adjustment for the credit card loan portfolio. | Note 13, p. 258 |
| **Wholesale—allowance for loan losses** | **+2** | Cumulative adoption adjustment for the wholesale loan portfolio: an **increase**, partially offsetting the consumer reductions. | Note 13, p. 258 |
| **Consumer & Community Banking (CCB)—allowance for loan losses** | **−591** | Net adoption reduction disclosed in the CCB segment’s selected-metrics footnote, driven by residential real estate and credit cards. This is a **business-segment view**, not the Firmwide total. | CCB, p. 70, footnote (g) |
| **Firmwide retained earnings—TDR adoption alone** | **+446** | **After-tax** cumulative increase under modified-retrospective adoption on January 1, 2023. | Note 1, p. 173; Note 13, p. 256 |

The portfolio adjustments reconcile to the Firmwide amount: **−489 − 100 + 2 = −587**. The **−591 CCB adjustment overlaps with those portfolio figures** and should not be added to them.

**A separate retained-earnings figure needs distinguishing:** the statement of changes in stockholders’ equity reports **+449 million** as the cumulative effect of changes in accounting principles. That covers **both TDR guidance and portfolio-layer hedge-accounting guidance**, adopted on the same date; it is **not the TDR-only retained-earnings effect**. *(p. 169)*

The filing gives **three distinct scopes** for customer pickup and delivery locations:

| Business scope | Pickup locations | Delivery locations and service | Reference |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Walmart globally** | **“over 8,000”** pickup locations | **“6,000”** delivery locations; not specifically labeled same-day | Item 1, “The Development of Our Company,” p. 6 |
| **Walmart U.S. segment** | **“approximately 4,600”** pickup locations | **“more than 3,500” same-day delivery locations** | Item 1, Walmart U.S.—“Omni-channel,” p. 7 |
| **Walmart International segment** | **“approximately 2,900”** pickup locations | **“over 1,900”** delivery locations; not specifically labeled same-day | Item 1, Walmart International—“Omni-channel,” p. 9 |

To preserve the qualifier wording precisely, the global sentence reads:

> “To date, we now have over 8,000 pickup and 6,000 delivery locations globally.”

The **U.S. and International counts are explicitly as of January 31, 2022**; the global statement says “to date.” These are service-location counts, not distribution, fulfillment, or sort-facility counts, and the global and segment figures should not be added together.

Source: *WMT_2022_10K.pdf*, pp. 6–7 and 9.

Apple’s fiscal 2023 Form 10-K identifies these causes of quarter-to-quarter differences in net sales:

- **Seasonal holiday demand:** Net sales have historically been higher in the first fiscal quarter than in other quarters.
- **New product and service introductions:** Launches can significantly affect sales. Their timing also affects indirect distribution channels: channels build new-product inventory after a launch, while older-product inventory often declines as a replacement approaches. Consumers’ and distributors’ anticipation of launches can also affect sales.
- **Dependence on a single product:** A significant portion of net sales comes from one product, so a decline in its demand could significantly affect quarterly sales.
- **Unexpected developments**, including:
  - Lower-than-anticipated demand for products or services;
  - Problems with new product or service introductions;
  - Information-technology system failures or network disruptions; and
  - Failure of a logistics, component-supply, or manufacturing partner.

**Sources:** *AAPL_2023_10K.pdf*, “Business Seasonality and Product Introductions,” printed p. 4 (PDF p. 7), and “Financial Risks,” printed p. 15 (PDF p. 18).

ExxonMobil’s **2025 Form 10-K gives four explicit annual dollar sensitivities**:

| Market price or accounting-assumption change | Stated annual dollar effect |
|---|---|
| **$1 per barrel change in Brent crude price** | Approximately **$700 million** effect on after-tax Upstream earnings |
| **$0.10 per MMBtu change in Henry Hub natural-gas price** | Approximately **$90 million** effect on after-tax Upstream earnings |
| **$0.10 per MMBtu change in Title Transfer Facility (TTF) natural-gas price** | Approximately **$20 million** effect on after-tax Upstream earnings |
| **Worldwide 0.5-percentage-point reduction in the assumed long-term return on pension-plan assets** | Approximately **$150 million increase** in annual pension expense, **before tax** |

**Scope and sources:**
- The three commodity-price sensitivities are estimates **for 2026**, covering Upstream consolidated subsidiaries plus equity companies and **excluding derivatives**. ExxonMobil cautions that benchmark-price movements are only broad indicators of actual earnings changes. *“Market Risks,” printed p. 62 (PDF p. 64).*
- The pension sensitivity is disclosed under *“Critical Accounting Estimates—Pension Benefits,” printed p. 67 (PDF p. 69).*

- **ExxonMobil:** The 2025 Superior Graphite transaction acquired **“key technology and assets,” not the entire company**. Pioneer and Denbury closed in 2024 and 2023, respectively. (*XOM_2025_10K.pdf*, PDF pp. 56, 114–115.)

For Berkshire, **OxyChem is excluded** because it closed on **January 2, 2026**, after fiscal year-end; the qualifying 2025 acquisition is **Bell Laboratories**. (*BRK_2025_10K.pdf*, PDF p. 80.)
